The role propelled Liotta to fame and earned him a Golden Globe nomination for best supporting actor. From there, Liotta starred as mobster Henry Hill in the Martin Scorsese classic "Goodfellas" (1990), working alongside renowned actors Robert De Niro and Joe Pesci. "Edgy guys stand out in people's minds," Liotta said of his famous "bad guy" roles, according to the Dispatch. But, to avoid being typecast as the "bad guy" forever, Liotta decided to break from the mold in his next role as a caring father in the heartwarming film "Corrina, Corrina" (1994), co-starring Whoopi Goldberg. Liotta soon proved that acting was not his only forte. He formed his own production company in 2002 and made his debut as a producer on the film "Narc," in which he also starred as a corrupt cop. He's also earned plaudits for his television work. In 2004, Liotta starred in an episode of the hit NBC drama, "ER," winning an Emmy for his guest appearance. The actor got his start on daytime TV, playing the character Joey Perrini on the soap "Another World." With several films currently in production, Liotta shows no signs of stopping. The actor told the Dispatch that he hopes to try his hand at romance in the future, joking that he'd like to "kiss the girl without having to choke her first." CNN's David Daniel contributed to this story.

The film became one of the most beloved sports fantasies of its era, and Liotta’s quiet, ghostly presence showed he could bring restraint as well as force.

But it was **Martin Scorsese’s “Goodfellas”** in 1990 that cemented Liotta’s place in film history.

As **Henry Hill**, the real-life mob associate whose rise and fall anchors the film, Liotta delivered the defining performance of his career. His narration helped drive the movie’s restless energy, while his performance captured both the glamour and terror of life inside organized crime. The film is now widely regarded as one of the greatest crime movies ever made.

Liotta’s final stretch in “Goodfellas,” as Henry becomes increasingly paranoid and desperate, remains one of his most recognizable screen moments. It also established him as an actor uniquely suited to characters living on the edge of panic and self-destruction.

## A career of cops, criminals and conflicted men

After “Goodfellas,” Liotta continued to move between leading roles and supporting parts, often playing cops, criminals or men caught somewhere in between.

In **“Cop Land”** (1997), he appeared alongside Sylvester Stallone, Robert De Niro and Harvey Keitel in a gritty police corruption drama. In **“Hannibal”** (2001), he took part in one of the film’s most infamous scenes opposite Anthony Hopkins. He also appeared in **“Blow”** with Johnny Depp and **“Heartbreakers”** with Sigourney Weaver and Jennifer Love Hewitt, showing a willingness to shift between crime, drama and comedy.

One of Liotta’s strongest later performances came in **“Narc”** (2002), in which he played a volatile undercover detective opposite Jason Patric. The film returned him to the morally murky world of law enforcement and crime, earning praise for its grim atmosphere and Liotta’s bruising performance.

He also became familiar to a different generation through his voice work as **Tommy Vercetti** in the video game **“Grand Theft Auto: Vice City.”** Released in 2002, the game became a cultural phenomenon, and Liotta’s performance helped give the main character a sharp, cinematic identity.

On television, Liotta won an **Emmy Award** for his guest role on **“ER,”** further proving his ability to make an impact even in a limited appearance.

## Facing off with Seth Rogen

In “Observe and Report,” Liotta’s Detective Harrison is not there to indulge Ronnie’s fantasies. He represents the actual police force, and his presence makes Ronnie feel threatened. That conflict gives the movie some of its sharpest moments, as Ronnie’s dream of becoming a real cop runs up against Harrison’s skepticism and authority.

The pairing works because Liotta brings credibility to the role. He has played enough detectives and criminals that audiences immediately understand what kind of man Harrison is supposed to be. He is professional, impatient and not easily amused — especially by a mall security guard who thinks he belongs on a major investigation.

Rogen, best known at the time for comedies such as **“Knocked Up”** and **“Pineapple Express,”** plays Ronnie as unstable and grandiose rather than simply goofy. Liotta’s grounded toughness gives the film a necessary counterweight.

Their scenes together turn the movie into more than a broad comedy. They become a collision between fantasy and reality — Ronnie’s fantasy of heroism and Harrison’s reality of procedure, authority and consequence.

## Still unpredictable

By 2009, Ray Liotta’s career had already included iconic films, cult favorites, crime dramas, comedies, television and video games. His role in “Observe and Report” may not be his largest, but it fits neatly into the larger pattern of his work: characters who bring tension the moment they enter a room.

Whether playing Henry Hill narrating his own downfall, Shoeless Joe stepping out of a cornfield, a corrupt cop, a haunted detective or a hard-nosed investigator in a mall comedy, Liotta has rarely been forgettable.

In “Observe and Report,” he once again proves that sometimes all a movie needs is Ray Liotta walking in, looking angry and letting everyone know the situation just got more serious.
